title: Your own data
text:
Terms on this page






fingerprint: a short code computed from the data, stored with each decision so it cannot be attached to a different version.
precision and recall: of what you found, how much was right; of what was there, how much you found.
stratified sample: a sample built slice by slice so the hard cases are represented.
frontier model: a model at the leading edge of capability; used here in a coding agent to write and repair the pipeline.

All terms: glossary.
The published session description invited you to bring messy historical datasets. An hour is not enough to work on them together, but the sequence transfers. Here is how to start, in the order that worked for Imperial Careers.

title: Your own data
text:
Before you open a model

Pick one question and one small sample. Twenty records you can check by hand beat two thousand you cannot. Include at least one hard case.
Keep the source reachable. Every record needs a reference that gets a reader back to the page: volume, page, line or offset. If your text came from OCR, keep the page images available. You will need them.
Decide what a record is. A person? A posting? A mention? Imperial Careers has one person per resolved biography and one event per posting, and the difference between “entry instances” and “people” is the whole of step 4.
Decide what the output looks like. A map, a timeline, a network. Build it early, from the first sample. It is your error detector.

title: Your own data
section: Rules that saved the project trouble
text:
Rules that saved the project trouble

Local identifiers first. Every record gets a stable local id before any external one. Add a Wikidata link only after retrieval and review support it. Nothing suitable? Keep the local id.
No identifiers from memory. A model will offer plausible Q-numbers. Treat any identifier that was not retrieved by a tool as unverified.
Ground to the historical entity, not the modern one. The Colony of Victoria, not the state; British Raj, not India. Where a surface means different places for different people, resolve per person, not per string.
Ties resolve to no merge. A missed link is recoverable. A false merge can silently corrupt later analysis.
Model decisions and human decisions in different columns. Never overwrite one with the other. Export human decisions with a fingerprint of the data they were made on.
Fix the rule, not the record. Then look at everyone the rule touched.
Make the correction a test. The probe that found the defect goes into the test suite.
Report what the sample can support. Handpicked cases explain failure modes. A stratified sample measures precision for one stratum. Recall needs labelled true matches, including ones the system missed. An oversampled stratum is not the population; report its result separately or weight it appropriately.

title: Your own data
section: Tools, and what they cost at scale
text:
Tools, and what they cost at scale
Two different jobs need two different kinds of model.

The agent that writes the pipeline reads your sample, proposes the structure, writes and tests the scripts, builds the review views and the atlas. This is hours of a frontier model’s time per project, in a coding agent. Imperial Careers used Claude in Claude Code.
The model inside the pipeline reads every entry and judges every cluster. At corpus scale, measure cost and throughput on a sample before choosing a model. Imperial Careers used Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a university GPU box for structuring, at about one entry a second, and Qwen3.8-27B on a Compute Canada cluster for the never-biographied matching, with the frontier model’s in-session work as the reference set to measure it against.

The agent can write the pipeline so that the cheap model does the reading and the agent is only called back when something fails. Which operation produced a given record should remain visible in the output.
For your first trial, you do not need a university GPU. Use twenty records you can check, a hosted model or your existing coding agent, and a small output table. Record input and output tokens, charges, elapsed time, failures and review time. University computing also has a cost even when there is no bill per request.
Take-home instruction for your agent:

Read these twenty raw entries. Explain which parts Python rules can handle reliably and which clauses need interpretation. Propose a hybrid approach, a schema and two example records before processing the rest. Keep a local record id and a source reference. Preserve the wording; put interpretations in separate fields. Show omissions, unresolved cases and validation failures. After my review, write a script that saves each result and can resume without repeating completed records.

The presenter’s environment uses Claude Code as the coding agent and the WikidataMCP server for lookups. Any coding agent that can run code, read files and call a lookup tool will do. See Run it yourself.

title: Ground
text:
Terms on this page






grounding: linking a name in the source to a shared identifier for the thing it names.
QID: a Wikidata identifier: Q plus a number, such as Q1800510.
vector search: search by meaning rather than by matching letters; the WikidataMCP server offers it over Wikidata.
MCP: a standard way of giving a model a tool it can call, so answers come from retrieval rather than memory.
gate: a rule that accepts a link only when the evidence leaves no plausible alternative, and otherwise leaves it unlinked.
surface: a place name exactly as printed, before any decision about what it refers to.
cache: the saved results of earlier lookups, keyed by the printed name.
API: a way for a program to send a request to a service and get an answer back; here, to a model or to Wikidata.

All terms: glossary.

title: Ground
text:
Why ground at all
Every arc on the atlas needs a latitude and longitude for a place named in a Victorian reference book: the Colony of Victoria, the Central Provinces, British Guiana, a princely state. Modern gazetteers do not have them or mislocate them. Wikidata has an item for each, with coordinates or a link to the capital that has them. For accepted place links, a query can retrieve coordinates or a capital. Unresolved names remain unplaced, and the choice of a historical entity and a period-appropriate seat still needs checking.
The second reason is composition. A historian of the Cape and a historian of Bombay who both ground to Q1800510 have joined their datasets without meeting. The longer argument is Jim’s; the short version is: ground to Wikidata, do not host your scholarship there.

title: Ground
section: Two ways to get a QID
text:
Two ways to get a QID
Retrieve it. The pipeline uses the WikidataMCP server’s vector search, which matches meaning rather than strings, then reads the item’s statements, then applies verification gates (type, dates, place) before accepting. Every accepted link has the retrieved evidence and the lookup date beside it. The Colonial Office List graph has 1,066 of its 27,526 person records grounded this way (about 3.9%), and 131,343 events grounded to a place. The gate aims to avoid false matches; that is a design aim, not a demonstrated zero-error rate. Low coverage matters: the linked people are not a representative sample of the roster.
Ask a chatbot. Paste the biography into a model with no tools and ask for the QID. It will give one. Sometimes it is right.

A third run, GPT Astra 6 at the medium setting with web retrieval, took 27 minutes and produced a structured file of 180 entities with offsets, confidence, a relation type, rejected candidates with reasons and dated evidence (scoring). All 155 identifiers passed the saved label/alias check; that check does not establish that every match fits its historical context. The file still maps one colonial Victoria to the modern state, and its “Malay States” match needs review. At about 80 seconds an entry, a serial extrapolation over 27,526 people is about 25 days. The place counts use different units and are not comparable accuracy scores. Even a retrieved, correctly labelled item can be the wrong historical match.
Use retrieval on hard cases and a reference sample, then have a historian review the decisions before treating them as a standard. Record wall-clock time, model charges and human review time separately. A slow demonstration is evidence about this run, not a general price comparison.

title: Ground
text:
Three questions to keep separate

Does the identifier resolve to what was retrieved? A Q-number from a model’s memory is not a lookup.
Is that entity the one in this source? Name, type, dates, place, activity. A real item can be the wrong person. Price’s item has the right dates and no career; the match rests on a rare name and Colombo.
What does the link assert? That this entry is that man. Not every statement on the item. Not that “Ceylon” in 1880 is the modern state.

title: Ground
text:
Places are harder than people
The surface “Victoria” occurs in the corpus as the Australian colony, the capital of British Columbia, an electoral district, a gaol in Hong Kong, a district in the Cape, a county in Mauritius, and a town in the Seychelles. The grounding cache (rows) shows what that took: the bare surface grounded to the colony by default, context rules for officials whose other postings are in British Columbia, manual re-grounding for the Cape and Seychelles variants, and six surfaces deliberately left ungrounded because one QID would be wrong for someone.
You decide: supported, unresolved, or wrong, for each link that matters, and the gate that decides the rest. The cases the gate gets wrong are the subject of the next step.
Next: The map finds the errors.

title: Structure
text:
Terms on this page






JSON: a plain-text format for a record: named fields in braces, lists in brackets (see the glossary for Trimen’s).
prompt: the written instructions sent to the model with each entry.
regex grammar: pattern rules that match text by its shape, written in Python; the deterministic first tier.
validator: Python that checks every place and year the model wrote against the source and drops what is not there.
post-normaliser: Python that applies the systematic fixes found by the audit, logging each change.
vLLM: an open-source server that runs an open model on a GPU and answers like a commercial API.
GPU: the graphics card the model runs on; the model has to fit in its memory.
token: the unit a model reads and writes in, roughly three-quarters of a word.
reasoning mode: a setting where the model writes out its thinking before answering; off here, because it spent the budget and returned nothing.
frontier model / open model: frontier refers to leading capability; open refers here to downloadable model weights. These are different properties, not opposites. The project used a commercial coding agent and an open model inside the pipeline.
deterministic: done by fixed rules, so the same input always gives the same output; no model involved.

All terms: glossary.

title: Structure
text:
The shape of it
Structuring the biographies was never “send them to a model”. It was a hybrid, in three parts, and the same three parts ran twice: once for the Colonial Office List in June 2026, once for the India Office List a week later.

Python first. A regex grammar for the printed entry shape parses what it can. It is all-or-nothing: if any clause containing a year fails to parse cleanly, the whole entry is refused rather than half-parsed. A second Python pass expands the abbreviations it recognises (“Feb.” to “February”, “acctnt.” to “accountant”) and leaves everything else exactly as printed.
A model for what Python cannot do. Binding position to place to time span across run-on, elided, “ditto” and concurrent clauses. One entry in, one JSON object out. For the Colonial Office List the first residue went to a batch API with a cheap commercial model; the bulk of both corpora went to an open model on a university GPU.
Python again. A validator that checks every place and year the model emitted against the source text and drops what it cannot find there. Then a post-normalisation pass that applies the deterministic fixes found by the audit, logging every change.

title: Structure
text:
The schema
One object per entry: surname, given_names, birth_year (only if printed), education, honours with award years, events, and terminal. One event per posting: position and place as printed, year_start, year_end, place_inherited, is_acting, and civil or military. The agent and the historian settled it on a sample before any batch ran.

title: Structure
text:
The prompt, exactly as sent
The system message for every one of the 65,000 entries (file):
You convert ONE printed Colonial Office List biographical entry into a JSON career record. Extract ONLY what is printed; never invent or infer facts.
Rules:
- events: one object per distinct posting. EXPLODE compound/concurrent clauses into separate events (e.g. 'reg.-gen., 1887, and M.L.C., 1889' = two events; 'ag. comsnr., 1915-16; and from 1919' = two events).
- position: as printed (the normalized expansion is fine), e.g. 'assistant colonial secretary'.
- place: the colony, territory, OR locality named in the clause, AS PRINTED (e.g. 'Ceylon', 'Negombo', 'N. Nigeria'). If the clause names no place, carry over the previous clause's place and set place_inherited=true; do NOT guess or upgrade a locality to its parent colony — record exactly what is printed. Inheritance stops when a transfer is stated.
- year_start/year_end: the posting's years; year_end null if a single year.
- is_acting: true when the post is acting ('ag.'/'acting').
- org_type: 'military' for army/navy/regiment/expedition/campaign postings, else 'civil'.
- honours: decorations/orders with their AWARD year if printed in parentheses (e.g. 'C.M.G. (1905)'); these award-years are NOT career events.
- birth_year: only if explicitly printed ('B. 1872'); else null. NEVER infer from the earliest career date.
- education: the 'ed. ...' string as one metadata string; university class honours stay here, NOT as events.
- terminal: {kind: retired|resigned|died|pensioned|other, year} if the entry states the career ended, else null.

Return ONE JSON object with EXACTLY these top-level keys: surname, given_names, birth_year, education, honours, events, terminal. Split the headword into surname + given_names (no 'name'/'person' key). Each honour is {"award": str, "year": int|null} (no 'decoration'/'order' key).

The user message is the entry alone, after the abbreviation pass. Trimen’s 1889 entry goes in like this (file):
TRIMEN, HENRY, M.B. (Lond.), F.R.S., F.L.S. —Formerly lecturer on botany at St. Mary's Hospital, London, 1867 to 1875; was senior assistant to department of botany, British Museum, 1869 to 1879; director Royal Botanical Gardens, Ceylon, February, 1880; author of numerous works and papers on pure and applied botany.

Three things to notice. Every rule in the list exists because an earlier run broke it; the rule about birth years is there because a model had been inferring them from the first appointment. The last paragraph pins the key names, because a bake-off found the model drifting to name and decoration without it. And nothing in the prompt is about the historical question; it is entirely about what the page says and how to hold it.

Three of the findings, source beside record (saved):
The ditto that was not resolved. Balmer’s last clause, “senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935”, came back with place: "do.". The rule says inherit; the model copied the abbreviation.
The appointment date that became a birth year. “BLAKELY, DONALD QUENTIN.—Clk., atty.-gen.’s off., B. Honduras, Apl., 1898.” came back with birth_year: 1898 and an event with no year. The prompt forbids exactly this. The same record expanded “off.” to “officer” instead of “office”.

title: Structure
section: Why the fix was not a bigger model
text:
Why the fix was not a bigger model
The errors are not random. They are a handful of systematic patterns: a short list of abbreviations mis-expanded the same way every time, ditto marks left literal, one compound honour split, “mentioned in despatches” dropped. Each has a deterministic fix, and those fixes are the post-normalisation pass: merge KT + BACH into Knight Bachelor; forward-fill a “do.” place from the previous event and set the flag; strip honorifics folded into given names; “officer in chief” back to “officer in charge”; drop a military tag with no military signal in the position. Every change is appended to a list on the record, so nothing is silent. The “off.” expansion is fixed one step earlier, by not pre-expanding ambiguous abbreviations at all.
The fixes do not establish the accuracy of the finished corpus. That needs a new audit after normalisation, including records changed by each rule and a fresh sample. A more capable model would also need that audit.

title: The atlas
text:
Terms on this page






coding agent: a model that can read files, write and run code, and call tools, rather than only answer in chat.
pipeline: the chain of scripts that turns the OCR text into the graph; run again when a rule changes.
arc: a line connecting recorded appointments; solid lines follow dated sequences, while dashed lines mark uncertain connections.
Wikidata item, QID: a shared identifier (Q plus a number) for a person or place, with its own facts attached.
F-score: one number for how much a system found (recall) and how much of that was right (precision); it does not give either value separately.
gazetteer: a list of place names with coordinates.
cache: the saved results of earlier lookups, so they are not repeated and can be corrected in one place.
re-emit: write the graph out again after a rule changes.

All terms: glossary.

title: The atlas
text:
Watch

This is an earlier atlas export, before the 7 October geography repairs. Fifty-six seconds. Each arc connects one official’s recorded postings between colonies, presidencies or provinces, drawn from the career graph and played out by year, 1815 to 1966. The interactive atlas behind it lets you search a name, follow a career, and open 186 proposed links between people in the Colonial and India Office records: Philip Edmond Wodehouse, Governor of British Guiana, then the Cape, then Bombay, is one of them, and a historian of the Cape and a historian of Bombay would each have known half of him.
The cross-service links are candidates: the September review found errors in a small check (11 of 15 links supported). Wodehouse is the worked example here; the full set of bridges needs further review.

The video is an earlier export; use the table above for the September build counts. These arcs represent sequences of recorded postings, with many points placed at an administrative seat. They are not observed travel routes.
Every arc lands where it does because a place name printed in a Victorian reference book was linked to a Wikidata item that carries coordinates, or links to the capital that does. Every arc belongs to one person because forty annual entries were resolved to one biography. Every arc has a year because a clause like “ag. comsnr., 1915-16; and from 1919” was read as two events, not one. Those are the three questions of the hour, and each was decided tens of thousands of times by a model and a few hundred times by a historian.

title: The atlas
section: From a visible error to a repaired atlas
text:
From a visible error to a repaired atlas
The atlas’s own panel for the same record, captured before the repairs on 7 October 2026:

These are the saved before rows. Each led to a published correction:

1858, “employed on a special mission” → Union of South Africa. The source says Venezuela. Venezuela is not a colony, so the event had no colony of its own and fell through to the next one. The rebuilt atlas uses the explicit Venezuela location and no longer fills a missing location from the nearest appointment.
1861, “high commissioner” → Union of South Africa, seated at Bloemfontein. The Union dates from 1910. In 1861 he was high commissioner for South Africa, from Cape Town. The surface “South Africa” was grounded to the twentieth-century state; the period entity is the office, not a polity. This one was made by a fix: the South Africa repair in step 6 sent the bare surface “South Africa” to the Union for every year.
1851, “Honduras” → seat Belmopan. A capital founded in 1970. The dated seat rule now places this appointment at Belize.

The India Office record had a fourth error: “superintendent of Honduras” inherited British Guiana, because its place was left empty and the inheritance rule filled it from the wrong direction. All four are now repaired in the public atlas. The build uses explicit grounded places, checks dates, and never fills a missing location from the nearest appointment. British Honduras uses Belize City for these dates. The wider audit checks both Lists and records corrections separately from candidates needing source review.

title: The atlas
text:
The loop
The project did not go OCR, extract, visualise, publish. It went round a loop, many times:

Build the pipeline with a coding agent: segment the biographies, structure them, resolve duplicates, ground the places.
Extract the whole corpus with a cheap model inside that pipeline.
Visualise the result in the form the research question needs.
See what is wrong. A premier of British Columbia sitting in Australia. South African postings landing at Harare. Two Baluchistans.
Fix the cause: a grounding rule, a mistaken inheritance, or a source-specific reading. Record the evidence and add a check.
Rerun and re-emit, and look again at everyone the fix touched, not only the case you noticed.

The atlas is step 3 and step 4 at once. It was built to answer a question about imperial mobility; it turned out to be the project’s best error detector, because a wrong grounding is invisible in a table of 180,000 rows and obvious on a map. Step 6 walks through three of the errors it found.

Trading Consequences, 2013
Imperial Careers, 2026




Structuring
A six-stage pipeline adapted by computational linguists; a relation was “same sentence”
A schema and a prompt written with a coding agent in an afternoon; a Qwen model reads 100,000 entries inside the script


Grounding
GeoNames string matching; “Saharunpore” missed because the gazetteer knew “Saharanpur”; a bug put every “Italy” in a Texan town. F-scores of 0.62 for commodities and 0.61 for locations, combining precision and recall

Review
Historians spotted false positives through the visualisations; false negatives were invisible
Same. The atlas found the errors; a sampled audit measured the rest



What changed is who writes the pipeline and how fast the loop from error to fix runs. What did not change is that the errors you can see get fixed, the errors you cannot see need a sample, and a corrected error should become a rule.

One dataset, start to finish
Two printed reference works, the Colonial Office List (1862–1966) and the India Office List (1886–1947), carry a terse biography for every senior official: born, schooled, every posting, every honour. The same man recurs in forty annual editions. The OCR garbles a name here and there. Two men who share a surname threaten to collapse into one career.
Over a few months, one historian with a coding agent turned those volumes into a knowledge graph and an animated atlas of imperial careers:

title: Glossary
text:
A plain-text way of writing a record so that every programming language can read it. A record is a list of named fields inside braces; a list is inside square brackets; text is in quotes; numbers and null (meaning “not given”) stand alone. Trimen’s entry, structured:
{
  "surname": "TRIMEN",
  "given_names": "HENRY",
  "birth_year": null,
  "education": "M.B. (Lond.)",
  "honours": [{"award": "F.R.S.", "year": null}, {"award": "F.L.S.", "year": null}],
  "events": [
    {"position": "lecturer on botany", "place": "London", "year_start": 1867, "year_end": 1875},
    {"position": "senior assistant to department of botany", "place": "British Museum", "year_start": 1869, "year_end": 1879},
    {"position": "director Royal Botanical Gardens", "place": "Ceylon", "year_start": 1880, "year_end": null}
  ],
  "terminal": null
}
That is what the model is asked to return for each entry, what the Python validator checks against the source, and what the graph is built from. One object per line in a file is a corpus; a spreadsheet can be made from it in one command, and the reverse.

title: Glossary
text:
The model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
The open-weights model used in the saved structuring runs. “35B” refers to total parameters and “A3B” to the approximate number active per token in its mixture-of-experts design. Fewer active parameters reduce computation; the other weights still need to be stored.
The project served it with vLLM on a university GPU box. The India Office List run processed 30,496 entries in 8.24 hours, with reasoning off, temperature zero and sixteen workers. Those are measurements of this setup and corpus, not a speed guarantee for another machine. The saved structuring page describes the prompt, checks and failures.
Two jobs. The coding agent writes and repairs the scripts with the historian. The model inside those scripts reads the collection. They can be different models. A more capable model can also help review difficult cases, but its answers need checking before becoming a reference set.

Starting without a university GPU
Use a small sample with a hosted model or an existing coding agent before choosing infrastructure for the whole collection. The same prompt can be tried through a hosted endpoint; the Imperial Careers comparison script illustrates that approach. Recheck output quality when changing the model or serving setup.
Local or rented GPUs are alternatives once the workload is clear. Memory requirements depend on the stored weight precision, context length and concurrent requests; weight size alone does not establish that a run will fit. A compressed model also needs a fresh check against the source sample.


A small cost worksheet
For twenty representative entries, record:







Measure
Why keep it

University allocations consume resources even without a per-request invoice

A successful response is not the only work you paid for


Human review and correction time
Cheap extraction can still produce expensive cleanup


Records accepted after review
Compare cost per usable record



For a rough token-cost estimate, multiply measured tokens per entry by the intended number of entries and the current input/output rates. State the assumptions: longer entries, tool calls, retries and a different mix of hard cases will change it. The model’s price is only one part of the project’s cost.

title: Glossary
text:
Other terms
F-score. One number summarising two: precision (of what the system found, how much was right) and recall (of what was there, how much the system found). The F1 score is their harmonic mean; 0.6 does not imply that either component is 0.6. Trading Consequences scored 0.62 on commodities and 0.61 on places.
QID. A Wikidata identifier: the letter Q and a number, such as Q1800510 for Philip Wodehouse. Stable, language-neutral, and shared by everyone who grounds to Wikidata. A model’s memory of one is not a lookup.
Grounding. Linking a name in your source to a shared identifier for the thing it names. The pages distinguish retrieving a candidate, reading its statements, and deciding the match.
Vector search. Search by meaning rather than by matching letters: the query and every item are turned into lists of numbers that place similar meanings near each other. “Walpole Island” by string finds an island in New Caledonia; by vector it finds the Ontario reserve. The WikidataMCP server offers this over Wikidata.
MCP. Model Context Protocol, a standard way of giving a model a tool, such as a search endpoint, that it can call and whose results come back as evidence rather than memory.
vLLM. An open-source server that runs an open model on a GPU and answers requests in the same format as the commercial APIs.
Mixture of experts. A model built from many small specialist networks, only a few of which run for each token, so it is cheap to run for its size.
Quantisation. Storing a model’s numbers at lower precision (4 bits instead of 16) so it needs a quarter of the memory, at a small cost in quality.
The three chatbots in the grounding test. Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google’s fast, inexpensive tier), Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic’s frontier model) and GPT Astra 6. All three were given the same prompt and the same twenty entries on 7 October 2026; Gemini without tools, the other two with web search.
Reasoning mode. A setting where the model writes out a chain of thought before answering. Helpful for hard questions; on this task it spent the whole budget thinking and produced no record.
Regex. A pattern language for matching text by shape (“capital letters, comma, names, a dash, then clauses ending in a year”). The project’s first tier.
Validator. Python code that checks the model’s output against the source and drops anything the source does not contain.
Ledger. An append-only file of decisions with reasons, such as the 917 merge groups, so that every decision can be revisited.
Silver standard. A set of cases labelled by hand after the fact, used to measure what the automated passes did. Here “silver” means a provisional reference set. Its value depends on how the cases were selected, labelled and checked; a frontier model’s answer alone is not a gold standard.
Conservative matching gate. A rule intended to accept a link only when the evidence strongly supports it, and otherwise leave it unlinked. The project calls this a “zero-false-positive gate”; that names an aim, not a measured guarantee. It trades coverage for precision, which is why a review queue exists.

text:
Terms on this page






cache row: one saved lookup: a printed place name and the identifier it was matched to.
manifest join, containment: matching printed names against a table of historical polities; accepting a match because one name occurs inside another.
ledger, dossier: the file of merge decisions with reasons; the evidence laid out for one cluster.

All terms: glossary.
Start with R1, R3 and R8 after you have decided. The other cases are further practice. These are the preparer’s answers with the evidence; each decision is for the proposal in front of you.

title: Worked answers
section: R1 (Structure). Blakely’s record does not stand
text:
R1 (Structure). Blakely’s record does not stand
Reject. The entry prints no birth clause. Its only date, “Apl., 1898”, is the appointment, and it went into birth_year while the event lost its year. The prompt forbids exactly this inference. Also “off.” became “officer”. This record contributed one of eight major findings across six records in the 186-record audit; the category is HALLUCINATION. The fix is a guard: a birth year may only come from a printed “B.” clause, and an event with no year while the entry has an unassigned date is flagged.

title: Worked answers
section: R3 (Clean). Abery and Carbery are one person
text:
R3 (Clean). Abery and Carbery are one person
Accept the merge. The rules allow a merge on an OCR surname variant when the forename and career are consistent and one identical dated event is shared. Here: same forename, same qualification (M.B.C.M.), the same 1867 Ceylon appointment, and ABERY attested only in the 1897 edition where CARBERY also appears. The ledger records the reason: “ABERY is OCR garble of CARBERY”. A reviewer who wanted more could check the 1897 page image for the lost characters.

title: Worked answers
section: R8 (Ground). Harris can be linked without settling his birth year
text:
R8 (Ground). Harris can be linked without settling his birth year
Accept with the disagreement recorded, or leave unresolved with a specific next check. The retrieved candidate shares the full name, Christ’s College and the Newfoundland governorship. Those support the identity despite the conflicting dates. A conservative reviewer can reasonably ask to see the scan and another independent account before accepting.
The proposal keeps birth_year_as_printed: 1858, records the external value 1855 separately, and flags the conflict. Accepting the link does not authorise changing the source field. The OCR could be wrong, the printed book could be wrong, or the external record could be wrong. The excerpt alone cannot decide which.
Next checks: inspect the 1927 page image, compare another edition, and trace the external date to its cited source. Do not count repeated copies of the same account as independent corroboration. Retrieved evidence.

title: Worked answers
text:
Further practice

R2 (Structure). Balmer’s “do.” is not a place
Reject as it stands; accept once resolved. The clause names no place; the rule says inherit the previous one, which is the Kenya-Uganda-Tanganyika service. The model copied the abbreviation. Because this error is systematic across the sample, the fix is a deterministic forward-fill: any place equal to “do.” or “ditto” inherits the previous event’s place, with place_inherited set. No model rerun needed.


R4 (Clean). A’Beckett and Beckett are two people
Reject the merge. The cluster exists only because of the suffix key and the forename. Birth years are 62 years apart, and the conflicting careers support keeping them separate; the year discrepancy is not the sole reason. The careers share nothing: Lincoln’s Inn and the Victorian bench against Nigerian telegraphs. This is the normal case in the cluster sample: the clustering is deliberately loose so that real variants meet, and most clusters resolve to “keep apart” in seconds.


R5 (Ground). “Union of S. Africa” is not Q5155572
Reject. Q5155572 is the British South Africa Company’s territory, seated at Harare. Q193619, the Union of South Africa, is what the surface names. The error came from a containment match on the string “South Africa” during the manifest join; it affected 960 Colonial Office events and was visible on the atlas as a Rhodesia node with far too many arcs. The fix patched five cache rows with a stated reason, and added a containment guard to the join. The October rebuild added the date-aware check: pre-1910 records cannot use the Union, explicit towns are retained, and unresolved jurisdictions are not replaced with a guess.


R6 (Ground). Brewster’s “Victoria” is British Columbia
Reject the proposed grounding; ground to British Columbia for this person. Every other clause in the entry is British Columbia, and Victoria is its capital and an electoral district. A surface-keyed cache cannot know that; a per-person resolver can. That repairs the geography only. The saved graph still turns the 1912 defeat into an appointment lasting to 1916; the source does not support that office held. Keep or type the defeat separately, and flag the appointment assertion for correction.
The place fix routed “Victoria” through a context rule (British Columbia signal in the career → Q1973, which geolocates to its seat; otherwise the Australian colony). Fixing it exposed a second bug: per-person overrides had never applied because the resolver and the graph keyed people differently. Both corpora were re-emitted.
What remains open: six “Victoria” surfaces (“Victoria district”, “Victoria county”, the Cape variants) mean different places for different people and are left ungrounded by design until each is resolved per person.


R7 (Ground, extra). Price is Q123279571, on the name and dates
Accept, with the evidence recorded. The item has a rare name with the alias covering the spelling, birth and death years consistent with the career (scholarship 1875, writership 1878), and a Tamil description meaning Sri Lankan politician, which fits three terms as mayor of Colombo. It has no career statements, so the match rests on name, dates and place of activity, and the record should say so. The pipeline’s conservative matching gate rejected it because the name spelling differs; that is the gate doing its job, and this is the kind of case a human review queue exists for. A reasonable person could also mark it unresolved pending a Ceylon directory; what they cannot do is treat the gate’s rejection as evidence that no item exists.

title: Worked answers
text:
The pattern
Across these cases the decisive evidence was never the model’s confidence and never the identifier’s existence. It was the source’s own words (“Apl., 1898” is an appointment; “do.” is a ditto), the dossier’s dates and careers, the item’s statements read rather than assumed, and the map. A correction needs a reason, a rerun and a check of other affected records. The ditto replay demonstrates that on a small sample; the Wodehouse and Brewster repairs show the same loop in the public atlas, including a wider check of affected records.

OCR: optical character recognition: software that turns a scanned page into text; its mistakes are the “garbles”.

title: The source
text:
The Record of Services
From 1883 every Colonial Office List carries a section headed, in most years, “Record of the Public Services of Officers”: between 1,400 and 2,900 entries per edition, cumulative, each a compressed career. Here is the 1889 entry for the director of the botanic gardens at Peradeniya:

TRIMEN, HENRY, M.B. (Lond.), F.R.S., F.L.S. —Formerly lecturer on botany at St. Mary’s Hospital, London, 1867 to 1875; was senior assistant to department of botany, British Museum, 1869 to 1879; director Royal Botanical Gardens, Ceylon, Feb., 1880; author of numerous works and papers on pure and applied botany.

The same man has an entry in seven editions, 1883 to 1896, and they differ (all seven). Later entries are denser:

BALMER, F. E.—Dep. chief acctnt., G.P.O., E. Africa Prot., Mar., 1919; ch. acctnt., G.P.O., Kenya, Oct., 1919; ch. acctnt., Kenya-Uganda-Tanganyika post and tel. service, 1933; senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935.


CONNOLLY, HON. SIR JAMES DANIEL, KT. BACH. (1920). —B. 1870; ed. Warwick Pub. Schl. and Catholic Schl.; M.L.C., Western Australia, 1902; col. sec. and min. of com. and lab., 1906; col. sec. and min. of pub. health, 1910; leader of leg. coun. from 1906 to 1911; M.L.A. for Perth, 1914; agt. genl. in London for Western Australia, 1917-23; agt. gen. in London for Malta, 1930.

title: The source
section: What the source can tell us
text:
What the source can tell us
These are administrative accounts of careers. They make offices, promotions and honours visible through the categories of colonial government. They are not a census of everyone who worked for, lived under or resisted those administrations. Repeated entries can repeat an error as well as confirm a fact.
The map adds another interpretation: a posting becomes a point, often at a capital, and successive postings become an arc. That point is a plotting location, not evidence that the official lived there; the arc is not an observed travel route. Keep the printed wording, the inferred location and the reason for the inference separately.

title: The source
text:
Why this example

The entries are formulaic enough that a schema is obvious, and irregular enough that every tenth one breaks it.
The same person recurs across editions, so identity has to be resolved before anything can be counted.
The places are nineteenth-century polities, not modern cities, so grounding is a historical decision, not a lookup.
There is a payoff at the end that depends on all three being right.

Next: Structure.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
Terms on this page






deterministic pass: a merge rule with no model: same name and birth year, or same name and a shared dated event.
cluster: a small group of biographies that might be one person, assembled by a loose key so OCR variants meet.
dossier: everything the project holds on the biographies in a cluster, laid out for one decision.
ledger: an append-only file of decisions with reasons, so each can be revisited.
silver standard: cases labelled by hand afterwards to measure what the automated passes did.
OCR garble: a name misread by the scanning software: ABERY for CARBERY.

All terms: glossary.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
The problem
Trimen has an entry in seven editions. A long-serving official has one in forty. Across 85 volumes the Record of Services yields 199,099 printed entry instances that have to be resolved into 27,526 people. Most of that is easy: the same surname, the same given names, the same career a line longer each year. The rest is where the OCR has rewritten a surname, a man has changed his title, or two men share a name.
The design rule, stated before any code was written (approach):

A missed link is recoverable; a false merge silently corrupts the record. Every default resolves ties to no merge.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
The passes

Deterministic passes merge on strong keys: identical name and birth year, identical name and a shared dated event, and so on. They did most of the work.
Clustering the residue: biographies that share a spelled forename and the last four letters of the surname land together, so OCR variants of one person meet.
Adjudication of each cluster by a model reading a dossier: every version of every biography, with birth year, education, honours, the full dated career. The output is a partition into people with a reason for each merge, appended to a ledger (rules and loop, first 25 ledger entries). 917 groups so far.
A silver standard of 200 hand-labelled cases, built afterwards, to measure what the passes and the judge actually did. On the India Office List the deterministic tier scored 39 of 40 (one unsure).

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
The rules
Merge only on positive same-person evidence: an overlapping dated event, a near-identical education string, a shared honour with its year, or an OCR surname variant with a consistent career. Birth year is OCR-noisy and never splits on its own. Different spelled forenames keep people apart. And the decisive case: same name, adjacent birth years, divergent education or specialty is two people.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
Four clusters
From a sample of twelve, unedited:








Cluster

Decision




ABERY, Joseph / CARBERY, Joseph
Both M.B.C.M.; both “1867 Ceylon Assistant colonial surgeon”; ABERY appears in one edition, CARBERY in six
Merge. ABERY is an OCR garble; the shared dated appointment, forename and qualification support the merge


A’BECKETT, Thomas, b. 1836 / BECKETT, Thomas Rumbold, b. 1898
Suffix and forename match; a Victorian judge knighted 1909 and a Nigerian telegraph engineer of 1948
Keep apart. Birth years 62 years apart and disjoint careers


ABRAHAM, Henry Charles, b. 1887 / GRAHAM, Charles Drummond, b. 1901
Suffix “aham” and the forename Charles
Keep apart. Different first forenames, different colonies, no shared event


ABBOTT, Myles John, b. 1906 / IBBOTT, John Thomas
Suffix and a shared “John”
Keep apart. Hong Kong judge of the 1930s and a Demerara customs clerk of 1860



Three of four are easy once the dossier is in front of you, and that is the point: the model’s job was to assemble the dossier and make the argument. The ledger keeps the reason, so the next person can disagree with it.
You decide: the cases where the evidence is one shared event and a plausible OCR garble. Whether a peer’s family name and his title are one biography. Whether a “thin” fragment with a full given name and nothing else should join a career. Those went to a review queue ranked by how much the decision matters: career length, cross-colony span, seniority.
Next: Ground.

title: The map finds the errors
text:
Terms on this page






cache row: one saved lookup: a printed place name and the identifier it was matched to.
surface: a place name exactly as printed.
manifest join: matching printed names against a prepared table of historical polities.
containment match: accepting a match because one name occurs inside another; the cause of the South Africa error.
canonical: the one agreed entry for a thing, to which duplicates are folded.
re-emit: write the graph out again after the fix.
stratum: one slice of a sample, chosen to oversample the risky cases.
false negative: a link or merge that should have been made and was not; invisible on a map.

All terms: glossary.
A wrong grounding is invisible in a table of 180,000 rows. On a map it is a dot in the wrong hemisphere. The project keeps a running list of defects surfaced while building the atlas, and a review of 3 September 2026 that re-fetched every QID in the graph and loaded the atlas headlessly to look for more. The examples below follow the errors through to their published repairs. Saved outputs show the earlier state; the rebuilt atlas shows the result.

title: The map finds the errors
section: A premier of British Columbia in Australia
text:
A premier of British Columbia in Australia
Harlan Brewster’s 1918 entry (saved): newspaper work in New Brunswick and Boston, removed to British Columbia in 1897, elected for Alberni, “defeated by Sir Richard McBride, in Victoria, 1912”, re-elected at a by-election in 1916, premier of British Columbia 1916. The saved graph gave him two events as member for Victoria. The bare surface “Victoria” was grounded to the Australian colony, Q56850459, by the surface-keyed cache. The atlas showed a British Columbia premier with a seat in Melbourne.
Seen on the map. Cause: a cache keyed on the surface string, with “Victoria” resolved once for everyone. Fix: a per-person context resolver. If the official’s other postings signal British Columbia, “Victoria” is British Columbia (Q1973), which geolocates to its seat; otherwise the colony. Also found while fixing it: per-person overrides had never applied at all, because the resolver keyed people one way and the graph another. Repairing that fixed a second, unrelated split between the North-Western Provinces of India and of Ceylon. Both corpora re-emitted.

A plausible map can still be wrong
Now read the source again: Brewster was defeated in Victoria in 1912. In the saved graph, that clause became a legislative assembly posting for Victoria from 1912 to 1916. Correcting the place leaves an unsupported appointment on a plausible map.
Pause and decide: does this record stand after the geography is fixed? What must be preserved, and what must be removed from a table of offices held?
The rebuilt graph now preserves the defeat as an event of its own type and removes the office-held assertion. The public atlas lists it under other recorded events. The same check applies to explicit electoral-defeat events elsewhere in the corpus; military victories and resignations require different readings. A checked location is not a checked career.

title: The map finds the errors
section: The Union of South Africa at Harare
text:
The Union of South Africa at Harare
Five surfaces, “Union of S. Africa”, “S. Africa”, “S.A.” and two more, had been joined to the Wikidata item for the British South Africa Company’s territory, Q5155572, because the join matched “South Africa” by containment. 960 Colonial Office events, 283 arcs in and 289 out, plotted at Harare.
Seen in the September review, on the map, as a node with far too many arcs for Rhodesia. Cause: a containment match in the manifest join. Fix: five cache rows patched to Q193619 Union of South Africa and a containment guard added to the join. That first repair still treated pre-1910 “S. Africa” too broadly; the October date checks completed this part of the correction. The patched rows carry the reason (cache rows).
The 7 October audit found 1,120 pre-1910 Union assignments across both Lists. The repair removes the anachronistic jurisdiction, retains explicit towns where available, and leaves ambiguous cases unresolved. It also removes the nearest-posting fallback and selects seats by date. See the audit and review queue.

title: The map finds the errors
text:
Two Baluchistans
The colony layer had Baluchistan under Q843, which is Pakistan, for fifty India Office events, and a second Baluchistan node under a different QID. The atlas drew two nodes with the same label. Fix: one canonical entry in the colony table, the duplicate folded in.

title: The map finds the errors
text:
What a fix changes
A source-specific correction records its evidence; a shared rule is checked against everyone it affects. After each one the pipeline re-emits both corpora and the atlas is rebuilt. The review then checks two things: the cases the fix was meant to repair, and the previously accepted cases that changed. The second group is where new errors hide.
The same discipline for structure: the every-tenth audit’s error catalogue became a post-processing pass with tests, and the three name probes that found the dedup defects are regression tests. The probe that found the error is the test that keeps it out.
The October checks also tested the actual lines drawn in the browser. Cameron’s temporary Windward governorship remains on the map and connects to Gambia. His Ottawa conference visit remains a written event without creating a map stop. A missing line could otherwise make a sound appointment look as though it had been removed.

title: The map finds the errors
text:
What the map cannot find
False negatives. An official whose “Victoria” was left ungrounded does not appear anywhere wrong; he simply has no arc. A merge that should have happened leaves two short careers instead of one long one, both plausible. For those the project built the silver standards: 200 hand-labelled cases, stratified so that the risky strata (rare surname, overlapping eras) are oversampled, scored against the machine output. On the Colonial Office List never-biographied population the judge’s “different” verdicts in the rare-surname stratum turned out to have a false-negative rate of 76 per cent, which no map would have shown.
Now: the exercise. Work through R1, R3 and the new R8. Give each decision a reason; for an unresolved case, say what evidence you would seek. The other five cases are further practice.

title: Cleaning, Structuring and Grounding Historical Data
section: Too irregular for regular expressions alone
text:
Too irregular for regular expressions alone
A familiar historical problem: semi-structured data.
The fields recur. The wording and relationships vary.







Source wording
What needs interpretation




“do., 1935”
Which preceding place does this posting inherit?


“B. Honduras, Apl., 1898”
An appointment date; “B.” belongs to the place name


Trimen’s posts, 1867–1875 and 1869–1879
Two concurrent jobs, not one sequence



Finding a year is easier than deciding what it dates.

14–16. This is a source problem historians know well: recurring headings, names, dates and offices without a uniform sentence structure. OCR can add variation, but even perfectly transcribed entries contain elision, abbreviations, compound clauses and concurrent appointments. Regular expressions recognise specified patterns; increasingly elaborate rules did not cover the collection reliably. Python is still useful for segmentation, regular cases and checks. Explain the three rows: Balmer inherits the preceding service’s place; Blakely’s “B. Honduras” is British Honduras and April 1898 dates his clerkship; Trimen’s lecturer and British Museum posts overlap. The third example is in the saved Trimen source pack. The conclusion of our discussion was that Python rules alone were insufficient for this corpus. The hard part is binding the right position, place and date, not simply detecting a number.

Start by showing Claude Code the raw OCR
I began by showing Claude Code the raw OCR and discussing whether Python could structure it on its own. We read examples, discussed what a record should contain, and worked out where explicit rules would be reliable and where the text needed interpretation.

title: Structure
section: Why regular expressions alone were insufficient
text:
Why regular expressions alone were insufficient
This is a familiar problem for historians: semi-structured data. Names, offices, places and dates recur, but their relationships are expressed in varied prose. The irregularity belongs to the source as well as to the OCR.







Example
What a reading must establish




Balmer: “senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935”
The new position inherits the preceding place


Blakely: “B. Honduras, Apl., 1898”
“B.” abbreviates British Honduras; April 1898 dates the appointment


Trimen: lecturer, 1867–1875; British Museum assistant, 1869–1879
Two appointments overlap; one does not end when the other begins



A regular expression can recognise a year or a specified abbreviation. Binding that year to the correct posting, carrying a place across an omitted phrase, or separating concurrent jobs needs more context. A fixed grammar could handle the regular cases, but adding exceptions did not make it a reliable parser for the whole collection.
Python remained useful for splitting the input, parsing regular clauses, managing the run and checking outputs. We developed a hybrid so a model could read the difficult clauses within an agreed structure.

title: Structure
text:
Develop and check the hybrid
The collaboration with Claude Code produced the schema, Python stages and extraction prompt. We settled the fields on a sample, inspected example records against their source, and revised the rules. The in-session runbook records batches of reference examples followed by Python validation. The model inside the eventual batch script was Qwen; Claude Code was the environment used to develop the machinery.
The resulting workflow had three parts. It ran for the Colonial Office List in June 2026 and for the India Office List a week later:

Python first. A regex grammar for the printed entry shape parses what it can. It is all-or-nothing: if any clause containing a year fails to parse cleanly, the whole entry is refused rather than half-parsed. A second Python pass expands the abbreviations it recognises (“Feb.” to “February”, “acctnt.” to “accountant”) and leaves everything else exactly as printed.
A model for what Python cannot do. Binding position to place to time span across run-on, elided, “ditto” and concurrent clauses. One entry in, one JSON object out. For the Colonial Office List the first residue went to a batch API with a cheap commercial model; the bulk of both corpora went to an open model on a university GPU.
Python again. A validator that checks every place and year the model emitted against the source text and drops what it cannot find there. Then a post-normalisation pass that applies the deterministic fixes found by the audit, logging every change.
